strengths: Clear theoretical insight that standard RL optimizes a first-order approximation of the ML objective, formalized via Maclaurin expansion with well-motivated interpolation between RL and exact ML
Principled framework with unbiased estimator (Theorem 2) where increased sampling improves the objective itself, not just variance—elegant theoretical property with practical implications
Unified weight-function view (Section 5) providing valuable insight into different objectives (REINFORCE, GRPO, ML) and illuminating GRPO's inversion for high pass rates

Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse settings: controlled (ImageNet), infinite data (maze), data-scarce (GSM8K), and large-scale LLM training with multiple benchmarks showing consistent Pareto improvements
Simple practical algorithm (Algorithm 1) requiring only single-line modification to normalize by successful samples K rather than total N, minimal implementation overhead
Consistent improvements across all tested settings, achieving up to 20× test-time scaling efficiency with strong empirical evidence for both pass@1 and pass@k metrics
Clear presentation with logical progression from well-motivated problem through elegant theory to comprehensive experiments with good reproducibility details
weaknesses: Limited theoretical guarantees: no convergence rates, sample complexity bounds, or analysis of approximation quality for finite T relative to exact ML; missing variance analysis of proposed estimator

Estimator returns zero gradient when K=0 (no successes), creating potential gradient starvation on hard examples despite motivation to focus on them; bias implications for low pass-rate inputs not discussed
Restricted to binary reward settings with perfect verifier; applicability to continuous rewards, preference learning, or other RL domains unclear, limiting generalizability

Incomplete computational analysis: claimed '20× speedup' refers to post-training inference with perfect verifier, not training-time improvements; training cost identical to REINFORCE; no wall-clock time comparisons
Missing ablations and sensitivity analyses: control variate (Eq. 10) introduced without ablation, no systematic study of T selection, no variance comparison with baselines despite being central to RL

Incomplete experimental evaluation: no error bars or confidence intervals across random seeds, no statistical significance testing; ImageNet's artificial low pass rate (~0.1%) limits informativeness; GSM8K shows slower initial convergence

Limited empirical comparison with related work, particularly PKPO (which directly optimizes pass@k); justification for harmonic weighting over alternatives not discussed; gap between success-conditioned theory and practical approximation underexplored

strengths: Novel theoretical insight connecting standard RL to maximum likelihood via Maclaurin expansion; shows RL optimizes first-order approximation of log-likelihood objective
Practical simplicity: single-line change to advantage calculation (r-mean)/mean instead of (r-mean)/std, enabling immediate adoption
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse settings (differentiable ImageNet, procedural mazes, fixed datasets GSM8K, large-scale Qwen3 training) with consistent improvements
Strong empirical results: up to 20× test-time scaling efficiency gains, maintains pass@k without distribution sharpening, better scaling with compute
Rigorous theoretical development with Theorems 1-2 providing exact gradient identities and estimator-objective equivalence proofs
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters in appendices, promised code release, clear Algorithm 1 implementation
Insightful analysis of optimization dynamics: weight function interpretation, gradient norm concentration on hard tasks, maintains broader pass-rate distribution
Addresses well-motivated problem: standard RL fails to recognize importance of improving likelihood for hard problems
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Theorem 2 guarantees T=N unbiasedness, but practical Algorithm 1 achieves T=N-1 due to K=0 baseline handling; gap analyzed in appendix but deserves main-text prominence
Restricted scope: core theory limited to binary rewards (though M.4 extends to non-binary); doesn't directly apply to continuous/arbitrary-valued rewards which remain important in many domains
Control variate baseline (Eq. 10) lacks theoretical guarantees beyond empirical variance reduction evidence (Figure 28); optimality not established
Limited analysis of failure modes: paper focuses on successes but doesn't discuss when/why MaxRL might underperform or settings where GRPO/RLOO could be superior
Experimental baseline concerns: REINFORCE fails dramatically on some tasks (may be suboptimally tuned); Qwen3 experiments use modest 1000 RL steps; some comparisons relegated to appendix
Statistical rigor: most results lack error bars/confidence intervals; limited multiple random seeds across experiments; statistical significance testing absent
Presentation density: paper is long and complex (15+45 pages); key insights sometimes buried; notation switches between formulations (m_θ vs π_θ) could confuse

Incomplete scope discussion: computational overhead not analyzed; convergence rates and sample complexity bounds absent; off-policy extensions deferred; perfect verifier assumption not deeply examined
